title: Illegal alien ordered removed years ago charged in crash that killed newly engaged 23-year-old teacher
description: Cameron Lyon, a newly engaged Ohio teacher, was killed when a previously deported illegal immigrant allegedly flipped his SUV into oncoming traffic.
fullText:
A previously deported illegal alien allegedly drove drunk before flipping his SUV into oncoming traffic and killing a newly engaged Ohio teacher, authorities said.

Alvaro Uribe-Gonzalez, a 33-year-old Mexican national who federal officials say illegally returned to the U.S. after being deported, now faces aggravated vehicular homicide and other charges in the death of 23-year-old Cameron Lyon.

Lyon's fiancée, 23-year-old Abrielle Kerns, was seriously injured in the fiery Sunday evening crash on U.S. Route 33 in Fairfield County, according to her family.

The Ohio State Highway Patrol initially described Kerns' injuries as non-life-threatening, but relatives said she remained in intensive care "fighting to recover" as the family grappled with Lyon's death.

Illegal Immigrant Suspect Charged In Crash That Killed Police Officer And His Girlfriend

"This is an unconscionable tragedy because it was preventable," Republican Ohio gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy wrote. "This perpetrator shouldn't have ever been in our country, let alone permitted to remain here."

Ramaswamy pointed to Uribe-Gonzalez's alleged drunken driving and immigration history as he vowed to take action if elected governor.

"But he ended up driving drunk & killed an innocent young man in Ohio. I won't tolerate this in our state," Ramaswamy wrote. "So devastating. It doesn't have to be this way. I'll fix it in Ohio next year & will go hard as necessary."

The Ohio State Highway Patrol said Lyon was driving west when Uribe-Gonzalez's eastbound GMC Terrain went off the right side of the highway shortly after 6 p.m.

Dad Of Illegal Immigrant Dui Victim Issues Warning To Americans Over Lax Driver's License Laws

Uribe-Gonzalez allegedly overcorrected, veered across the roadway and overturned into the westbound lanes, slamming into Lyon's Chevrolet Trax. The GMC then caught fire.

Lyon was treated at the crash site but died a short time later, the patrol said. Uribe-Gonzalez suffered minor injuries.

Investigators said alcohol is suspected to have played a role in the crash.

Uribe-Gonzalez was charged with aggravated vehicular homicide, driving under the influence of alcohol and operating a motor vehicle without a valid license.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged a detainer with the Fairfield County Jail the day after his arrest, asking local officials not to release him before federal agents can take custody.

Illegal Alien Charged With Killing 4 Young People In Wrong-way Dui Crash On Oklahoma Highway

The Department of Homeland Security (Dhs) said Uribe-Gonzalez first entered the country illegally through Texas in January 2020 and was arrested by Border Patrol.

An immigration judge issued a final removal order Jan. 11, 2020, and the Trump administration deported him to Mexico April 14 of that year, according to DHS.

Federal officials said Uribe-Gonzalez later illegally crossed back into the U.S. at an unknown date and location.

"This illegal alien has been charged with aggravated vehicular homicide and driving under the influence of alcohol after allegedly causing a car crash that killed 23-year-old Cameron Lyon in Ohio," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

Ice Urges North Carolina To Keep Illegal Immigrant Charged In Triple-fatal Hit-and-run Behind Bars

"Cameron had his whole life ahead of him, and that life was stolen by this criminal who never should have been in our country in the first place."

Mullin said ICE wants Ohio officials to cooperate with the detainer so Uribe-Gonzalez can be taken into federal custody and removed from the country.

Lyon had recently begun his first teaching job and was well-loved by staff and students at Crestline Exempted Schools, according to a fundraiser for his family.

A graduate of Otterbein University, Lyon was remembered as a cherished son, brother and friend whose death left his family and community devastated.

title: Russia's Valieva loses neutral athlete status
description: Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva will not be able to compete internationally after the sport's governing body revokes her neutral athlete status.
fullText:
Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva will not be able to compete internationally after the sport's governing body revoked her neutral athlete status.

The 20-year-old returned to the ice in January after serving a four-year doping ban but remained ineligible for this year's Milan-Cortina Olympics.

Russian athletes have been barred from competing under their national flag since the country's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, although International Skating Union rules allow for Russians to compete as neutral athletes.

According to those rules, an individual is presumed eligible unless the ISU determines they are in active military/security service for Russia or Belarus, have taken part in military operations against Ukraine or have "publicly supported that war".

The ISU initially granted Valieva neutral status for the 2026-27 season but that has now been refused.

A video featuring Russian President Vladimir Putin is pinned on Valieva's Instagram account.

Russian men's skater Mark Kondratiuk, a team-mate of Valieva's at the 2022 Winter Olympics, has also had his status revoked.

Valieva was 15 when she helped Russia win team gold in Beijing, becoming the first female skater to land a quadruple jump during the Olympics.

But shortly afterwards it emerged that she had tested positive for heart medication trimetazidine - classed as a performance-enhancing drug - six weeks earlier.

A Russian Anti-Doping Agency (Rusada) investigation concluded Valieva bore "no fault or negligence" for the violation, but the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) upheld an appeal by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada).

Valieva and her team-mates were stripped of gold, with her ban backdated to when she tested positive in December 2021.

title: France wants to transform Fifa after withdrawing Infantino support
description: French football leaders have proposed to seek ways to transform how Fifa is run after the country's football body became the latest to withdraw support for Gianni Infantino's presidency.
fullText:
France's football leaders have proposed to seek ways to transform how Fifa is run after its national association became the latest to withdraw support for Gianni Infantino's presidency.

On Thursday, the French Football Federation (FFF) followed England, Italy, Republic of Ireland and Scotland in withdrawing support for Infantino over his aborted plan to sell stakes in Fifa competitions - including the World Cup - to private investors.

The FFF had pledged its support for Infantino in June before his investment proposal came to light.

Infantino's plan sparked a global outcry, with European football's governing body Uefa threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions.

Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and North American governing body Concacaf have called for Infaninto to step down, though he retains the backing of South America's Conmebol and African governing body CAF.

Fifa has confirmed Infantino will stand for a fourth term in the Fifa presidential election in March.

"A project with such a significant impact on the future of football could not be envisaged without comprehensive information, in-depth consultation and a fully transparent decision-making process," FFF president Philippe Diallo said in a statement.

"Fifa's governance does not live up to the standards that football represents."

Despite Infantino abandoning his proposal, the FFF said that "Fifa's governance cannot be considered resolved".

The FFF has pledged to start consultations with confederations, national associations, players, supporters and governance experts about reforming Fifa.

"The aim of these consultations will be to foster collective reflection and to draw up proposals for a far-reaching transformation of Fifa's governance, with a view to restoring confidence, enhancing transparency and ensuring the independence and exemplary conduct of world football's governing body," the FFF said.

"The FFF, a founding member of Fifa, thus intends to contribute to a debate that is vital for the future of football, its regulation and its development."

title: Okafor says he won't play for Swiss again under Yakin
description: Leeds United forward Noah Okafor says he will not play for Switzerland again while Murat Yakin remains as head coach.
fullText:
Leeds United forward Noah Okafor has announced he will not play again for Switzerland under the leadership of Murat Yakin, citing a breakdown in trust with the head coach.

The 26-year-old has earned 26 caps for the Swiss national team since making his debut in 2019 but only featured for 19 minutes at the World Cup, coming off the bench in their last-32 win over Algeria.

In a statement released on his Instagram account on Thursday, Okafor said his decision was unrelated to his lack of game time, instead attributing it to how he feels he has been treated by the current leadership.

"My decision has nothing to do with my playing time," Okafor wrote. "Things happened that hurt me deeply. Trust was broken. Commitments were not kept.

"When I was allowed to play against Algeria, people reacted to minor mistakes far away from our goal in a way that hurt me deeply.

"In the weeks that followed, I thought a lot and decided for myself that I no longer want to play for the national team under the current manager."

The Swiss FA was informed by Okafor on Thursday, with a spokesperson telling Reuters: "We respect his decision and wish him every success with his club."

Switzerland are next in action on 26 September, travelling to North Macedonia for their opening match of the 2026-27 Nations League.

Okafor joined Leeds from AC Milan in August 2025 for £18m.

Yakin has been head coach of Switzerland since August 2021.

title: In Michigan, GOP Senate candidate makes a Canadian-sized gamble on trade
description: Former Rep. Mike Rogers is trying to stake out a nuanced position on President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada, which will have a disproportionate effect on his state.
fullText:
GOP candidates in states bordering Canada are running far away from President Donald Trump on trade. Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers, however, is taking a more nuanced — but politically risky — approach.

The former representative, who's locked in a heated race for Michigan's open Senate seat, is arguing that some of the tariffs Trump imposed on Canadian goods last month are "necessary," as he said in a recent statement — a nod to the state's manufacturing sector, which has been gutted by cheap foreign imports in decades past.

At the same time, he's suggesting he has the pull to help bring an end to the trade war that threatens his home state, which does roughly $80 billion in trade with Ontario, Canada, each year, according to the Michigan Chamber of Commerce .

That's a contrast with other northern Republicans running for Senate this fall like Sen. Susan Collins in Maine and former Sen. John Sununu in New Hampshire, who have unequivocally condemned Trump's escalating trade war. Even Rep. John James, the GOP nominee for governor in Michigan, has taken a more critical stance in recent days, saying in an interview he did not want the state to be "a pawn in these trade negotiations."

Rogers isn't the only GOP official attempting to straddle the line between defending his state's interests and defending one of the president's signature policies. But he may have the toughest time pulling it off of any of them, given the stakes for Michigan and for his Senate race, where Democrats are increasingly honing in on the Canada trade war.

"If you've gotta explain what's going on in tariffs, the longer you explain it, the more you're losing," Jim McFerran, chair of the Republican committee of Wayne County, which includes all of Detroit, warned in an interview. McFerran added that it's a particularly challenging issue for Republican candidates because the president has done a poor job of laying out how Canada has been an unfair trade partner for years. "It's too hard to explain because it hasn't been explained well."

Rogers' campaign referred POLITICO back to his August statement on Trump's Canada tariffs, as well as a recent announcement from Detroit-based auto manufacturer General Motors that it will shift $4 billion worth of production from Mexico to three different U.S. plants, including one in Orion Township, Michigan, which the campaign indicated was a product of Trump's trade agenda.

Rogers has also tried to link the trade conflict with Canada with the threat of cheap auto imports from China, arguing Beijing could use the United States' northern neighbor as a conduit to flood American markets.

But despite supporting some of Trump's protectionist trade policies, leading voices in Michigan's auto sector are condemning his newest trade war.

United Auto Workers "rejects any escalation on Canada, a country with strong unions and labor standards," the union's president, Shawn Fain, said in a statement on the new U.S. tariffs on Canada that went into effect last month. "If we're going to increase tariffs anywhere, it should be on countries where automakers continue to offshore jobs because they can pay workers $3 an hour, force them to work in unsafe conditions, and crack down on independent unions."

An auto industry executive, meanwhile, said Trump's threat to hit Canadian auto and parts imports with a 50 percent tariff on Jan. 1 would be "cataclysmic" for the sector.The person was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the president's policies.

Roughly $1.3 billion in Michigan exports face Canada's new counter-tariffs, according to a POLITICO analysis, one of the highest amounts of any state. And many of the state's largest employers, including automakers, the dairy industry, appliance manufacturers and other industrial suppliers, all stand to take a particular hit from the duties, which stretch from 15 to 50 percent.

"Products will move back and forth across the Michigan-Ontario border, potentially multiple times during the food production process," said Chuck Lippstreu, the president of the Michigan Agri-Business Association. "That underscores the importance of the two-way trading relationship with Canada … especially for a border state like ours that also sits on one of the busiest trade corridors on the continent."

That's also true for the auto industry, which represents roughly a quarter of the state's gross domestic product and employs hundreds of thousands of people. Parts and manufacturing of many leading American vehicles take place on both sides of the border — Ford's F-Series Super Duty truck, for example, is made in a new plant in Oakville, Ontario. Its transmission comes from Ohio. Its axles come from Michigan. Its engine comes from Ontario.

The tariff tit-for-tat with Canada "further undermines [Republicans'] ability to make a strong argument on the affordability issue, given the impact that it is likely to have and has had over the last several months," Jason Roe, a Michigan-based GOP strategist who used to be executive director for the state Republican Party, said in an interview.

Given that economic reality, Roe said he suspects "the administration would probably give Michigan Republicans a little bit of latitude" to break with the president on the tariffs the way other border state GOP candidates have in recent weeks.

Collins has been unstinting in her criticism while campaigning in Maine over the weekend, while contradicting White House claims that the tariffs won't hurt the U.S. The administration, she said in an interview, "has very much underestimated the impact on Maine families, on small manufacturers, on our agricultural products. … They look at this issue as a macro issue. And in fact, the micro-impact on a state like Maine is considerable."

Collins was one of the few Republicans who has consistently spoken out over the past year against Trump's tariffs, not just on Canada but on other major trading partners and allies like the European Union, Mexico and Japan. Most GOP lawmakers have maintained that the duties are a necessary but temporary part of Trump's negotiating strategy.

Michigan Republicans, too, have been trying to have it both ways on tariffs, said Jarrett Skorup, a spokesperson for the Mackinac Center for Public Policy, a free market policy think tank based in Michigan.

"They're trying to kind of take a middle ground, like we gotta have a good trade policy because other countries are harming us, but they also aren't necessarily defending all the tariffs," said Skorup, "particularly this latest round, which are leading to fights with Canada, because that is traditionally Michigan's No. 1 trading partner."

After Trump escalated trade tensions with Canada last month, many more Republicans are now raising public alarms.

Rogers, however, has not tried to create much daylight with the White House — on trade or otherwise. He attended a rally with Vice President JD Vance in Sterling Heights, Michigan, on Aug. 31 hosted by the pro-Trump super political action committee MAGA Inc. Rogers is also one of two Senate candidates with a confirmed speaking role at the midterm convention Trump is hosting later this week in Dallas.

In an interview last week on Fox News Channel's "Fox & Friends," Rogers argued that his relationship with Trump would help — not hurt — Michigan on trade. "You can send somebody back who gets up every day and tries to gouge the president's eyes out or you can send somebody back who's going to walk in and say, 'Hey, can we work on this part of the trade deal?' The Canadians have not been good partners on this," Rogers said.

When the president threatened to shut down a new bridge connecting Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, that was built to ease congestion and promote trade, Rogers voiced support. "Canada just took Chinese-made cars and dropped them down from 100 percent tariffs to a 6 percent tariff. I would like the president to have some leverage to stop thousands and thousands and thousands of Chinese-made cars pouring over the bridge," he said. "Do you know who that hurts? It hurts Michigan autoworkers."

Gus Ghanam, the chair of the Macomb County Republican Party in the suburbs of Detroit, said he thinks Rogers is right to stand with the president on trade policy, but acknowledged that trying to justify any jump in prices during an election is "a tough thing to say to somebody."

"The message should be, 'You might have a little discomfort now, but in the end, you're gonna be happy,'" Ghanam said.

It's a risky approach. Even before counter-tariffs went into effect Tuesday, Trump's approval in the state was sinking. A poll by Michigan State University conducted late last month found that only 34 percent of Michiganders view the president favorably. A statewide poll by EPIC-MRA around the same time found that 63 percent of respondents feel the national economy has gotten worse over the past year.

"Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he's asking Michigan families to pay the price," Abdul El-Sayed, Rogers' Democratic opponent in the Senate race, said in a statement. "Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long. Mike Rogers won't do anything but rubber stamp them."

El-Sayed has leaned into the issue in recent days, bringing up the tariffs last week when asked to respond to Vance's recent comments that "there's something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil." El-Sayed's campaign even released a "The Price is Wrong" video that parodies the long-running game show by asking voters to guess "just how much everything's gotten more expensive over the last year because of Trump's tariffs and his war in Iran."

"This is going to be felt up and down our state in a more significant way than others, and this is on the mind of virtually every single voter," said Lon Johnson, the former chair of the Michigan Democratic Party. "It's very important for Abdul to continue to drive that distinction with Rogers on this issue."

title: Aitchison to steer England in WXV opener
description: Holly Aitchison will win her 50th England cap when she starts at fly-half in the Red Roses WXV opener against Australia on Saturday in Manchester.
fullText:
Holly Aitchison will win her 50th England cap when she starts at fly-half in the Red Roses' WXV opener against Australia on Saturday in Manchester.

Aitchison, 28, started two of England's wins en route to their Six Nations Grand Slam earlier this year, but has been unable to supplant Zoe Harrison as head coach John Mitchell's pick at 10 for the biggest matches.

Aitchison is one of five changes to the England team that beat France in Bordeaux last time out.

Scrum-half Natasha Hunt makes her comeback from a knee ligament injury that has kept her out of action since the win over Ireland in April, while fellow World Cup winner Tatyana Heard makes her first Test appearance of the year after recovering from a foot injury.

May Campbell, whose five previous England appearances have come off the bench, makes her first Test start with resources stretched thin at hooker.

Amy Cokayne will miss the match through injury and Connie Powell is recovering from ankle surgery, while Lark Atkin-Davies is on maternity leave having had a daughter in June.

Their absences mean back-up hooker Bryony Field, who plays alongside Campbell at Saracens, is set to win her first senior England cap from the bench, where Hannah Botterman, who has not featured since 2025's World Cup final win, and Morwenna Talling are primed to make returns from injury.

Gloucester-Hartpury's Mia Venner, who finished joint top of last season's PWR try-scoring charts, come in on the wing.

Aitchinson, Heard and Talling all play for Sale Sharks, whose men's team host games at the CorpAcq Stadium, where Saturday's match takes place.

"It feels like a dream that my 50th Test is going to be in the north west," said Aitchison, who began her career at hometown club Firwood Waterloo, less than 40 miles away.

"It's the first time we've been here in, like, 20 years, so it's going to be magical."

Mitchell, who spent two spells with Sale as a player and a coach, is also relishing the return.

"I have very fond memories of the north west from my time with Sale Sharks so it's awesome to be able to take our game to this part of the country," he said.

"Playing in a different part of the country allows us to be present in the community and keeps the game healthy. You've not only got to be visible, but if you can actually be close to your community, I think that's even better."

Unlike England's men, who are tied to Twickenham's Allianz Stadium by the commercial advantages of staging matches in an 82,000-capacity venue owned by the Rugby Football Union, the Red Roses are regularly on the road.

England will take on Canada for the first time since victory in the team's meeting in last year's Rugby World Cup final at Exeter's Sandy Park next weekend, before finishing the home leg of the WXV Global Series against New Zealand at Allianz Stadium on 26 September.

Away matches against Canada (twice) and the United States follow in October as part of the new-look event which aims to fill out the women's Test calendar away from the World Cup.

Australia have named the uncapped Amelia Whitaker on the wing. Whitaker, 20, is the niece of former Australia and Leinster scrum-half Chris Whitaker.

Elsewhere, exciting 19-year-old Caitlyn Halse, one of a clutch of Australians to have signed for Leicester for the next PWR season, is included at full-back.

England have won all eight of the teams' previous meetings, most recently prevailing 47-7 in the pool stages of last year's World Cup.

title: Top four seeds in historic semi-final line-up
description: For the first time since 1975, the top four seeds in the women's US Open singles draw have reached the semi-finals.
fullText:
That was Coco Gauff's surprised reaction when she learned she was part of a US Open semi-final line-up that has not been seen in more than half a century.

For the first time since 1975, the top four seeds in the women's singles draw have reached the semi-finals at the New York major.

Now, 51 years later, the stars have aligned once again with Aryna Sabalenka, Elena Rybakina, Jessica Pegula and Gauff all surviving three-set thrillers to create a semi-final line-up for the ages.

"How amazing - it doesn't get much better than that does it?," former British number one Annabel Croft told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"It has felt fantastic the whole tournament - I just feel like I've been more enthused about looking forward to the match-ups this Grand Slam than any I can remember."

It is the first time the top-four ranked players have reached the women's semi-finals at any Grand Slam since Wimbledon in 2009, and it hints at a shift away from the unpredictable landscape that has characterised the women's game in recent years.

Since the start of 2020, there have been 13 different Grand Slam women's singles champions - compared to just seven on the men's side.

"I just feel like there's lots of really big names now, big personalities going up against each other and it's really exciting," Croft added.

"We've been blessed with the amount of intriguing matches we've had. You're seeing these warriors out on court."

Top seed and two-time defending champion Sabalenka will face American Pegula in Thursday's first semi-final (00:00 BST, Friday), while Rybakina - who will replace Sabalenka as the new world number one on Monday - takes on fourth seed Gauff afterwards.

While Sabalenka is bidding to become the first woman since Serena Williams in 2014 to win three successive US Open titles, Pegula is the only player remaining in the women's draw still chasing a maiden Grand Slam.

The pair need no introduction to each other, having faced each other 13 times.

That includes the past two US Open tournaments, when Sabalenka denied Pegula a first major title in the 2024 final and fought back to win in last year's semi-finals.

"It's fun to look at it like a rivalry. I think that's what motivates me," said Pegula.

"I know that she's definitely pushed me to become a better player, so I always respect and appreciate that aspect of our rivalry."

Pegula, who has got the better of Sabalenka on four occasions on the WTA Tour, said beating the four-time major winner at Grand Slam level is a "hurdle" she must overcome.

Sabalenka, meanwhile, said she was "super excited" to face Pegula, who arrived in New York in better form after reaching the final in both Washington and Cincinnati.

"I'm loving playing against her because it's a battle, because it's a fight, and I love being under pressure and going through tough challenges," said Sabalenka, who is into her first semi-final since falling to Pegula at June's Berlin Open.

"I know she hasn't maybe had the best results this summer, but I know that she has a lot of confidence playing here at this tournament, and she's going for a three-peat," Pegula added.

But the second seed has described the top ranking as "just a number" and stressed that her focus remains focused on winning her third Grand Slam title.

"It's never quite the same if you become world number one having lost a Grand Slam final or semi-final just beforehand, so she will be trying to cap off an absolutely perfect couple of weeks by winning the title," tennis correspondent Russell Fuller said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

Standing in her way, however, is Gauff, who will have the home crowd's backing on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The 22-year-old American, who won the Flushing Meadows title in 2023 but suffered fourth-round exits in the following two years, said she has a different perspective to this year's tournament.

"Sometimes you're just so focused on the now, now, now, because you want it now, and obviously you want to take advantage of your opportunities," she said.

"In the grand scheme of things, [I'm] definitely sitting here in a different mindset and perspective than I was last year.

"It inspires me a little bit more to keep working, as I see how much I have improved in a year."

Gauff leads the head-to-head 2-1, but Australian Open champion Rybakina fought back from a set down to triumph in last month's Canadian Open semi-finals.

"I'm going to have some aces hit on me and some winners hit on me, but I'm going to keep fighting and give it my all. That's all I can do," Gauff said.

title: Ukraine says AI is moving beyond drones and into strike missiles for the first time
description: Ukrainian defense firms have already widely incorporated AI into their drones, but little has been said about missiles.
fullText:
Ukraine is developing artificial-intelligence-enabled missiles, a first as its autonomous warfare evolves.

Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform, said multiple companies are part of this effort.

AI has already been widely incorporated into Ukrainian drones and robots.

Ukraine is developing strike missiles augmented by artificial intelligence, a first and a significant step as its offensive weapons become increasingly autonomous.

Brave1, the Ukrainian state-backed innovation platform, confirmed to Business Insider that multiple companies involved in this initiative are developing AI-enabled missiles.

Ukrainian companies have widely incorporated AI into their drones and war robots, enabling functions such as decision-making, navigation, and targeting. Missiles are new.

"AI was initially deployed at scale in drones," Andrii Hrytseniuk, Brave1's CEO, told Business Insider. "It's not that fast — it's sufficient for the drones, but missiles require much higher speeds."

Hrytseniuk shared that AI is now "increasingly being integrated into missile systems as well. Although it hasn't reached the scale of hundreds of solutions seen in the drone sector, we are already seeing first successes and plenty of developments in progress."

More than 200 Ukrainian companies were developing AI-based parts for missiles, drones, radars, and other systems, Hrytseniuk said in an earlier interview in May.

Efforts to integrate AI into missiles appear to have ramped up as Kyiv invests in developing long-range strike weapons, often used to attack military and energy targets inside Russian territory.

Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's former defense minister who pushed for advances in battlefield innovation and just launched a high-profile venture fund in Kyiv to invest in military startups, said this week that one of his priorities is "low-cost strike missiles and, eventually, missiles powered by AI."

It's unclear how the Ukrainian companies are using AI in the country's missiles and how far along they are in the development process. The technology will add to Kyiv's capabilities, but won't remove humans entirely from the process, Brave1 said.

The approach echoes Ukraine's use of AI in warfighting systems more broadly. Both soldiers and defense companies have stressed that humans must remain involved in operations in some capacity, saying that drones can't act entirely on their own.

The war has become significantly more autonomous over the past year as Ukrainian and Russian drones flood the battlefield. They constantly monitor the front lines, creating a miles-wide "kill zone" where any movement could trigger a precision strike.

Ukrainian officials have set out to replace soldiers with ground robots and drones in particularly dangerous missions — such as casualty evacuation and logistics — whenever and wherever possible, reflecting the push to become more autonomous.

description: Does Mauricio Pochettino have a case that Tottenham should be retrospectively crowned Premier League champions?
fullText:
Should Tottenham be retrospectively crowned Premier League champions for the 2016-17 season?

That's the opinion of former manager Mauricio Pochettino, who led Spurs to a second-place finish - seven points behind Chelsea - that season.

This is about Chelsea making £47m in secret payments, according to a Premier League investigation, to unregistered agents and third parties to seal transfers between 2011 and 2018.

The transfers included Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o, Willian, Ramires, David Luiz, Andre Schurrle and Nemanja Matic.

Four of those - Hazard, Willian, Luiz and Matic - were at the club in 2016-17.

During that period Chelsea won two Premier League titles (2014-15 and 2016-17), two FA Cups (2011-12 and 2017-18), the EFL Cup (2014-15) and the Europa League (2018–19).

Chelsea have been fined by Uefa, the Premier League and the Football Association, but Pochettino thinks that is not enough.

"If they admitted they broke the rules, the Premier League title was for the second-best team," Pochettino said.

Pochettino is one of the first people of significance to articulate what many feel - that Chelsea got off lightly with a fine.

Fans of Everton and Nottingham Forest have pointed out that their clubs faced points deductions for relatively small profit and sustainability breaches, while Chelsea sought to sign star players with secret payments.

Meanwhile, there is no sign of a verdict in the case of Manchester City's 115 charges for alleged breaches of Premier League financial rules.

Does Pochettino have a point? And how much of an impact did those four players have on the title race?

Hazard is seen as the poster boy for Chelsea's breaches.

The Blues fought off most of Europe's top clubs to sign him from Lille for £32m in the summer of 2012.

Between May 2013 and August 2016, according to the investigation, seven payments totalling £5.6m were made to an unregistered agent "for the benefit of the club in connection with Hazard's transfer".

Pochettino's argument is that Spurs could have beaten other clubs to the signing of players of similar ability had they also ignored the rules.

What about Hazard's impact in the 2016-17 season?

The Belgium forward started 36 Premier League games, scored 16 goals and provided five assists. Only Cesar Azpilicueta started more matches, and only Diego Costa netted more goals (20).

Hazard was Chelsea's player of the year, was named in the Professional Footballers' Association (PFA) team of the year, and made the shortlist for PFA player of the year.

Then there's the direct impact of his goals and assists in the results of four fixtures.

Hazard scored the first goal in a 2-1 win over West Ham in August, then scored a goal and provided an assist in a 2-0 victory over Southampton in November.

In March he scored the opener as Chelsea again beat the Hammers 2-1, and got both goals in a 2-0 win over Manchester City in April.

You could argue that input was worth 10 points.

There is no doubt that Hazard had a huge influence, but this was his fifth season at the club. It was not as if Chelsea signed him in the summer of 2016.

Willian joined Chelsea from Anzhi Makhachkala in 2013, with the investigation finding that transfer fee payments totalling £19.2m were made to two unregistered entities in connection with his move and that of Samuel Eto'o.

Willian was not a regular starter in 2016-17, with 19 of his 34 appearances coming from the bench.

But he still had a huge influence, scoring eight goals and providing eight assists.

The Brazilian's attacking returns were crucial in four matches.

He had an assist in a 1-0 win at Sunderland in December. He scored two goals in a 4-2 victory over Stoke in December, and the first goal as Chelsea beat Stoke 2-1 in March. He provided an assist for the winning goal in a 4-3 victory over Watford in May.

His contributions helped Chelsea take eight points from those fixtures.

Crucially, Chelsea nipped in at the last minute to sign Willian from under the noses of Spurs, who might argue that was only because of the secret payments.

The investigation found that Chelsea made payments totalling £5.1m between 2012 and 2015 "to provide talent identification services in certain European countries".

This was identified as payments in relation to the registrations of Ramires, Luiz, Schurrle and Matic.

However, by 2016-17 Matic and Luiz were in their second spells at Chelsea. The deal with Benfica which meant Matic and Luiz swapped clubs in 2011 was looked into.

Matic returned to Stamford Bridge in 2014, with Luiz having a spell at Paris St-Germain from 2014 to 2016.

While the deals that took the players back to Chelsea were not specifically referenced, the association was created.

Matic played 35 league games in 2016-17, including 30 in the starting XI. He scored one goal and set up seven.

Only one of those attacking contributions influenced a result, but that was an assist for Chelsea's first goal in a 2-1 win over Tottenham in November.

Luiz, who was named in the PFA team of the season, started 33 matches and scored one goal - the opener in a 1-1 draw at Liverpool in January.

How Chelsea signed a star team with hidden payments

Chelsea fined but avoid suspended points deduction

Tottenham were relentless at the end of the 2016-17 season, winning 12 of their final 13 matches to finish on 86 points.

Yet Antonio Conte's Chelsea were almost as relentless, winning 11 of their last 13 to take the title with 93 points.

Spurs' tally would have been enough for the title in 2015-16, when Leicester finished on 81.

However, since 1999-2000, when Manchester United were champions on 79 points, 86 points would only have won the title twice, including the two most recent seasons.

Tottenham's problem in 2016-17 was too many draws at the start of the campaign. Despite an unbeaten 11-game start, only five of those were victories.

Chelsea lost more matches - five to Spurs' four - but secured 30 wins to Tottenham's 26.

Pochettino might argue that the attacking influence from Willian and Hazard proved the difference, with those two players having attacking contributions in eight different matches which led to points.

Then there is the mere aspect of sporting advantage - how the signings of players like Hazard enabled Chelsea to win trophies, qualify for the Champions League and therefore attract more top talent.

Pochettino feels he should have a Premier League title to his name.

Remember that he managed Chelsea for one season, when he struggled to win over supporters.

Chelsea finished sixth in 2023-24, but neither Pochettino nor the club are likely to look back fondly on that period.

It is different at Tottenham, with the Argentine still adored for his five-year spell in charge from 2014.

As well as finishing as Premier League runners-up, he took the club to the Champions League final in 2018-19.

The 86 points earned in 2016-17 is a club record too.

So do Spurs fans share his view?

"Of course I do," said Chris Paouros, co-founder and co-chair of Proud Lilywhites, external and Women of The Lane., external

"He could tell me the moon was made of halloumi and I'd nod along.

"The Spurs 2016-17 team was the best in the league by most measures: best attack, best defence, fewest defeats, unbeaten at home in the last season of the old White Hart Lane.

"If the playing field was tilted, the least you can do is ask the question."

Paouros knows Spurs will not be handed the title, but said the "rules have to mean something, whoever benefits".

There is another side to this, however.

If you get given a title a decade later because of a rule breach, could you celebrate it?

"It would still be something that Spurs fans would celebrate," said Tristan Foot, secretary of the Tottenham Hotspur Supporters' Trust. "A victory over Chelsea, albeit 10 years after the event."

But that sense of injustice is still there for other Premier League clubs.

"It means that to an extent crime does pay in football," Foot said. "And that's the serious underlying part all of this.

"During the transfer window they were signing players that we had no chance of winning, the obvious example being Willian.

"The Premier League has got to be better about imposing sporting sanctions and making sure that its rules actually have teeth."

With all investigations now concluded, it seems unlikely that Pochettino - or anyone else - will get a retrospective trophy parade.

Will clubs get that same feeling when the Manchester City saga is finally over?

title: Arsenal close to finalising new contract for Arteta
description: Mikel Arteta is believed to be close to finalising a new contract with Premier League champions Arsenal.
fullText:
The perception of Arsenal's transfer window varies depending on who you speak to - but there will be no disagreement from anyone at the Emirates Stadium over how crucial their next expected signing will be.

With the market closed until January, the club are now in the process of finalising an agreement with manager Mikel Arteta over his protracted new contract.

Well-placed sources indicate those discussions have moved forward recently amid full confidence from those involved in talks that the Spaniard will renew.

Indeed, Arteta moved unequivocally last month to remove any lingering doubt over his future: "Everybody feels comfortable that the timing of the contract is not going to be an issue because my will certainly is to be here and I'm very happy here.

"My feeling from the club is the same one. That's why everyone is doing things in a very organic way."

Similarly, Arsenal's chief executive Richard Garlick has said it was merely a "matter of time" before Arteta's new long-term deal was confirmed.

Arteta can expect to become one of the best paid managers in world football once his new contract is signed - Arsenal committed to significantly improving on his current deal, worth £10m a season plus an extra £5m upon Champions League qualification.

For Arsenal supporters, the official announcement can't come soon enough, particularly given his current deal now has just nine months left to run.

Since his appointment in December 2019, Arteta has transformed Arsenal from a club that had lost its Champions League status to one that won the Premier League for the first time in 22 years last season.

They are overwhelming favourites to retain their domestic crown and are fancied to win their first-ever Champions League this season.

With that success comes power. Like Arsene Wenger before him, Arteta is categorically the most influential figure, certainly from a football perspective, at the club.

People will say that the manager or head coach should always be the most authoritative figure at any football club - the reality is that is rarely the case.

Arteta's fingerprints are all over the club - and most importantly the squad. Nothing happens from a first-team perspective without his approval.

When Arsenal tried to sign Julian Alvarez and Vinicius Jr last month, it was Arteta who was at the forefront of the club's charm offensive.

With that in mind, the thought of removing Arteta from that dynamic, certainly for Arsenal's ownership, is the unthinkable.

One day, Spain will come calling - and a return to his homeland may attract Arteta, although he knows he is unlikely to be afforded the same authority at either Real Madrid or Barcelona – clubs that are historically entrenched in internal politics – than he is now.

But at this moment, the attraction for Arteta is with Arsenal.

This is a squad that has flourished under Arteta's tutelage. The average age of the squad (26.2 years) is one of the oldest in the Premier League. It's a group at its peak and primed to build a legacy on.

Beyond the new financial terms and into footballing ambition, Arsenal are buying into Arteta's vision.

The summer arrivals of Bruno Guimaraes and Ezri Konsa were sizeable investments given both turn 30 next year, while the albeit failed pursuits of Vinicius Jr and Alvarez provided Arteta with evidence that the club's American owners are willing to spend heavily on elite talent.

It's the sort of ambition Arteta is understood to have made clear he wanted to see as talks over his contract progressed.

Arteta's six years at the Emirates already makes him the longest-serving manager in the Premier League and EFL by some distance - his new deal will take him closer to a decade in north London.

Yet there appear to be no signs of Arteta taking his foot off the gas.

title: 'Get a life' - non-league club condemn man impersonating manager
description: Gainsborough Trinity condemn a person who has been approaching players while falsely claiming to be their manager.
fullText:
A non-league club have condemned a person who has been approaching players to make transfer and wage offers while falsely claiming to be their manager.

Gainsborough Trinity, who play in the Northern Premier League Premier Division - in the seventh tier of English football - say the individual has contacted "a number of players" across different levels of the non-league pyramid.

Chief executive Matt Boles said he wanted to make it "categorically clear" communication over potential deals had not been from manager Russ Wilcox or on behalf of the club.

"We strongly condemn the actions of the individual responsible," he said on the Gainsborough club website, external.

"Impersonating a football manager and making false representations to players is completely unacceptable and has the potential to cause unnecessary disruption and reputational damage to players, managers and clubs."

Boles said Gainsborough became aware of the bogus approaches when managers, players and officials at other clubs contacted Wilcox directly, suspecting he was not behind the phone calls and messages.

BBC Sport understands an agent also reached out to Wilcox to share their suspicions after the imposter offered them an excessively high transfer fee for a player.

"Many have done so precisely because they know Russ, know the professional standards by which he conducts himself, and immediately recognised that this is not the manner in which he would approach or attempt to recruit a player," Boles said.

Wilcox told BBC Lincolnshire he does not know why anyone would behave this way.

"I don't want my reputation tarnished," he said. "I've been in the game 40-plus years and I've never had anything like this before."

Boles also issued a strong message to the person responsible for the hoax.

"Enough is enough," he said. "Stop impersonating our manager, stop wasting the time of players and clubs across the non-league game and, quite frankly, get a life."

Gainsborough, who reached the FA Cup second round in 2024-25 and first round last season under Wilcox, have made the Northern Premier League and Football Association aware of the incidents.

"It's quite serious. If we were speaking directly to a player, it's an illegal approach, it's tapping up and the club can get in trouble with the FA and the leagues," he told BBC Lincolnshire.

"More importantly for Russ, it's his reputation that's been dragged through the dirt.

"I don't get what [anyone] would achieve out of it. Just pack it in."

Wilcox has been with the club since 2023 following previous managerial spells at Scunthorpe United and York City.

He featured for Northampton Town, Hull City, Doncaster Rovers, Preston North End and Scunthorpe during his playing days.

title: One of McKinsey's top AI leaders explains how it's stopping staff from overspending on tokens
description: Debasish Patnaik, leader of McKinsey's UK QuantumBlack division, said the firm pings consultants about their AI usage.
fullText:
McKinsey advises some of the world's biggest companies on managing their AI spend.

Internally, the firm has implemented controls to help manage how its staff use AI tokens.

One solution is an email alert when consultants' AI usage gets too high.

Consulting firms moved quickly to make AI part of employees' working lives. Now they are confronting the cost of using it at scale.

One of McKinsey's strategies for managing rising costs isn't to cap consultants' use of AI but to let them know when they're using too much.

The firm tracks consumption on a user-by-user basis and alerts its employees via email when their AI usage gets too high, said Debasish Patnaik, who leads QuantumBlack — McKinsey's AI, data, and analytics group — in the UK. The alert system was introduced firmwide in the summer.

"Similar to using mobile data on a work phone, we tell them this is how you could do things to make it more cost-effective for the firm," said Patnaik.

Companies that initially focused on encouraging AI experimentation are now confronting the cost of operating the technology at scale.

The age of freewheeling AI token use came to an end earlier this year as LLM providers moved from subscriptions to consumption-based pricing models. Consulting firms and other enterprise users are now charged based on the number of tokens — the small chunks of text an AI model reads and produces — they use, rather than a flat access rate, making efficiency more important as usage grows.

In September, OpenAI announced that its most prolific users of AI coding agents now consume more than $7,000 worth of tokens a day.

McKinsey's approach to managing that spending pressure rests on transparency and education, Patnaik said.

The AI usage alerts aren't intended to discourage employees from using AI, but to show them what they are consuming and help them complete the same work more efficiently.

"We really believe in giving autonomy to the consultants," said Patnaik.

Ensuring they have the right education about how to use tools has been key for managing usage, he added, noting that McKinsey has already seen shifts in how employees use the tools since giving users more visibility into their AI habits.

McKinsey's internal AI spending has not yet reached a problem stage, Patnaik said.

title: Team GB return after pregnancy 'hard to put into words' - Kinsella
description: A year after giving birth, Alice Kinsella takes the latest step on her groundbreaking return to gymnastics at an international meeting for Team GB.
fullText:
Olympic gymnast Alice Kinsella says "it's hard to put into words" how she feels about returning to international competition as her groundbreaking comeback to the sport continues this weekend.

The two-time European champion became the first British artistic gymnast to resume elite competition after giving birth, when she finished fourth in the beam at the British Championships in March.

Now the 25-year-old is preparing for her first competition back in Team GB colours at a senior team international against France, Switzerland, Germany and Italy at Fenton Manor in Stoke on 12-13 September.

"It's kind of crazy - it's such a surreal feeling but I am very excited," Kinsella told BBC Radio Stoke.

"It's only been a year, postpartum. Training-wise, it's been tough, but it's been good. I'm excited to finally get out there. I'm ready, I'm doing everything I can to get back where I was.

"It's been a rollercoaster but a good one."

Kinsella's pioneering journey back to the sport is so rare it became the subject of a university research paper into elite gymnasts resuming their careers after giving birth.

Her son Parker, who was born in September 2025, is already a source of inspiration and he will be watching his mum compete at the weekend as Kinsella competes in all four pieces of apparatus - balance beam, bars, vault and floor - for the first time.

"It's really special because I've wanted to try to get back into a team and this is a really good start because it's a little four-way," Kinsella, who trains with Park Wrekin Gymnastics Club in Shropshire, said.

"It's not too big of a competition which is really good. I'm definitely nervous, but it's hard to put into words - it's been so long.

"I did the British [Championships] in March but only did beam and that's all I was training really but now I'm trying to do all four so it's more on the body.

"It's not like you've done one piece and you can stop thinking about everything, you've got to move on to the next and think about that. So it's been tough."

Pioneering gymnast targets rare return to elite competition after baby

'For my boy' - Kinsella makes GB gymnastics history

Gymnastics now more a mental challenge - Kinsella

After revealing she only took "three or four weeks off" after giving birth, Kinsella returned to training at the start of the year with the longer-term intention of being at the World Championships in China in 2027 and the Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028.

But, after finding herself ahead of schedule so far this year, she wanted to take the chance to step it up.

"My main goal was to try to get back next year but I'm actually a lot further forward than I thought I would be," added Kinsella, who won bronze in the team event at the Tokyo Olympics in 2020.

"So that's why I'm doing this competition because I just want to get out there, compete, because I don't like doing nothing."

What makes Kinsella's return so unique are the obvious challenges - and changes to the body - pregnancy and childbirth brings.

There are many examples of women returning to the top of their sports after becoming mothers but gymnastics, where vital pelvic floor and core strength are both weakened during pregnancy, is different.

Kinsella said her gymnastics background has played a big part in her being able to return to physical exercise so quickly but said she "didn't feel too bad" when she got back in the gym.

"I always had that goal to get back into the gym and I think when I've got a goal set I will do everything I can to achieve it," she said.

"Getting back into a leotard with how my body's changed just feels very weird but I guess that shows what my body has gone through and I try to think about it in a positive way."

Her body is not the only thing that has changed with Kinsella adding that parenthood has helped her become better at taking the pressure off herself as an athlete.

"Having a baby changes your life - I'm very patient, whereas before Parker I was not patient at all," she said.

"When I made one tiny mistake I would get so annoyed, but now if I just make like a little mistake I'm totally fine about it.

"You have to be patient with kids, they're crazy. So I've definitely changed in that aspect but style-wise and gymnastics-wise like I don't think that's changed.

"Things are harder to get back and to do but I think the more I train it'll probably feel a lot easier."

Kinsella said when she started her comeback "no one really had any idea what I was going to able to do" and wants to keep levels of expectation for her international return as realistic as possible.

For her, this weekend in Stoke is there primarily "just to enjoy it" and to "get the experience of all four pieces [of apparatus] again".

"My body's changed, I can't do the same amount of training I used to do but I'm definitely getting back to that," Kinsella said.

"We're definitely on the right track to be where I was before I had Parker. My goal was to start competing next year properly on all four.

"It's going to be really fun. Whatever happens, happens, good, bad. I'm just proud I'm able to be back out there a year postpartum."

title: Switch Six Nations fixture to USA to grow game – World Rugby
description: World Rugby would help any nation which wants to switch a Six Nations match to the United States as it continues its drive to spread the game stateside.
fullText:
World Rugby would help any nation which wants to switch a Six Nations match to the United States, as it continues its drive to spread the game stateside.

South Africa and New Zealand have sold out the 71,000-capacity M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore for Saturday's fourth and final Test in their Greatest Rivalry series.

With the men's and women's Rugby World Cups being held in the United States in 2031 and 2033 respectively, tournament organisers are keen to bring more prestige fixtures across the Atlantic.

"In terms of the match-day economics, [South Africa vs New Zealand] is like a Six Nations match," Alan Gilpin, World Rugby chief executive, told the Daily Telegraph., external

"It starts to show that [financial return] is not the barrier. So if there is the appetite to take some of these big matches in the future to the US, we can now."

The All Blacks have been at the forefront of rugby's attempts to make an imprint in a notoriously tough sports market.

Ireland memorably beat the All Blacks for the first time when the teams met in front of a capacity 60,000-strong crowd at Chicago's Soldier Field in 2016, with a 2025 rematch proving a similar commercial success.

New Zealand have also staged matches against the United States - a 104-14 victory in front of about 40,000 fans in Washington, external - and Fiji - a 47-5 win before 33,217 in San Diego - in the country over the past decade

However Gilpin believes that the history of the Six Nations and its ability to connect with expatriate fans in the United States could be a useful tool to crack America further.

"This isn't a live discussion of an Italy vs Ireland game, but why we use that as an example?" he added.

"You've got two fantastic fanbases in the US of Irish and Italian fans

"If you could take a Six Nations game to the right place, to a Boston or to a New York, where there's a lot of those fanbases, you can definitely drive the economics.

"Now, you're going to have Irish fans and Italian fans in those respective home countries saying, 'Hang on a minute, you know, we want to see our country play?'

"The counter-argument to that [is] it's still Irish and Italian fans getting the chance to watch their team, so they're just not the ones who live in Ireland and Italy on this occasion. But that's a balancing piece we've got to work through."

Wales played their home matches at London's Wembley Stadium during the 1998 and 1999 Six Nations while the Principality Stadium was being built, but such a long-haul venue switch would be unprecedented in the tournament's 143-year history.

England women's head coach John Mitchell, who led the United States' men's team earlier in his career, said he was unsure whether a stateside expansion would ultimately succeed.

"I've worked for America. I understand that geography," he told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"American sport is full of rivalries and I just don't think Americans adjust to new rivalries or new franchises compared to probably some of the other countries.

"Will rugby ever go big there based on its its early investment?

"I'm not sure I can answer that, but what I do know is that rugby union is a difficult challenge for large parts of America."

He was also wary of the prospect of a Red Roses' Six Nations match being staged in the United States.

"The visibility's huge here in the European market," added Mitchell.

"Let's use it because that's the way to grow the game slowly, rather than putting huge investments into something that might have potential, but not necessarily that visibility."

While World Rugby could support a stateside Six Nations game, the decision would lie with the competing teams, all of whom would be aware of the consternation that would come with transplanting a fixture thousands of miles away.

The schedule for the 2027 editions of both the men's and women's tournaments have already been set.

title: 'Waste of energy': Senate Democrats are sitting out the John Fetterman pile-on
description: The unpredictable Pennsylvania senator is absorbing a massive intraparty backlash. But not from his Senate colleagues.
fullText:
Sen. John Fetterman has faced a tide of public criticism from fellow Democrats as he stakes out lonely ground as a critic of the far-left wing of his party — and another wave rolled in Wednesday after he made a surprise video appearance at the Republican midterm convention.

So far, however, his Senate colleagues haven't joined the pile-on.

Democratic senators are staying above the fray as they work to flip the majority in November amid constant speculation that the 57-year-old Pennsylvanian could trigger a nightmare scenario by leaving the party and caucusing with the GOP.

Some have worked to publicly bat down suggestions that Fetterman could abandon Democrats for the final two years of his term — something he has denied considering, even as he continues to raise eyebrows with his outspoken support of Israel, bashing of democratic socialists and close relationships with Senate Republicans.

"John Fetterman is a friend and an important member of our caucus. It's a waste of energy to get spun up about his voting record or place in our party — he votes with us 90 percent of the time," Democratic Sen. Peter Welch of Vermont, who is close with Fetterman, said in a statement to POLITICO before the convention appearance. "We need a big tent if we're going to win in November."

That silence could be tested in the coming weeks. Recent reports, including in The Wall Street Journal, detailed how he has skipped meetings with key constituencies and largely stopped participating in caucus lunches or committee meetings. Fetterman denounced the report as "lies, half-truths, innuendos, [and] smears" peddled by "disgruntled staffers."

A social media account purported to be run by former Fetterman aides has teased the release next week of additional stories and evidence related to his job performance, which could spark a new wave of questions for the senator and his colleagues once they return Monday from a five-week summer recess.

Fetterman further fueled party-switch chatter with a recent appearance with Pennsylvania's Republican senator, David McCormick — then heaping praise on McCormick in the convention video Wednesday, where he also pledged to "work with" President Donald Trump to protect his state's steel industry.

In a statement Wednesday, Fetterman said his Republican convention remarks were intended to pay tribute to McCormick "as a great American and friend."

"We are in different parties, but we are both Team PA," he said. "We have delivered hundreds of millions of dollars back to Pennsylvania, fought for improved transportation and affordable housing, and the Steel Way of Life."

"I'm a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party — and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on," he added.

If any Democrats fear driving Fetterman into the GOP's arms with intraparty criticism, some of his potential 2028 competitors aren't among them.

Former Rep. Conor Lamb, who lost to Fetterman in 2022 and is mulling a 2028 bid, said in an interview that he's believed for close to a year that his onetime Democratic primary foe would become a Republican — a position he acknowledged puts him "in the minority."

"I don't think anything I say, or anyone who is a Democrat says, affects him all that much," Lamb said, adding, "The fact that the Senate Democratic leadership thinks they can keep them on their team by saying a few nice things about him in public just shows that they haven't learned who they are dealing with."

Pennsylvania Rep. Chris Deluzio, a Democrat who is also mulling a 2028 Senate bid, also shrugged off a question about if the public criticism of Fetterman — who he accused of "undermining our efforts to take back the House" — could drive the senator to become a Republican.

"In the two years he has left in this job, in this term, he should be a Democrat," Deluzio said. "That is what the people of Pennsylvania elected him to do. That is what they expect him to do, that is what I would say he should do with what he has left in the Senate."

Still, Senate Democrats have largely avoided casting aspersions. Republicans hold a three-seat advantage, and Democrats believe they are in striking distance of picking up the four seats they'd need to win control. A post-election Fetterman flip could put the Senate back to 50-50, giving Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote.

Multiple Democratic senators approached by POLITICO this week about Fetterman simply declined to comment. Asked in a late July news conference if he wanted Fetterman to stay in the party, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said he did.

"He is a very good member of Congress," he said. "The people in our caucus very much like him and respect him, and we're a big tent party. We can have a lot of different views in that party."

A Senate Democratic aide — who, like others quoted for this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly — said Democrats "are keen on batting down" the speculation that Fetterman would split from the caucus.

Fetterman has repeatedly downplayed that possibility. In May he wrote in a Washington Post op-ed that he had "no plans to leave" the Democratic Party and that he would be a "terrible Republican who still votes overwhelmingly with Democrats." In July, at the Hill Nation summit, he appeared to anticipate being a pivotal member of the party next year.

"If I was going to, I would have already done that," Fetterman said in July about a party switch. "And I would remind everybody, we are talking about how it's possible, how we could retain the majority in the Senate — well, that's because I make that mathematically possible. And if we flip those four seats, then I would be 51."

But he laid out a red line, saying there was "one condition" where he would abandon the Democrats — if they become "the anti-Israel party."

Privately, many Senate Democratic colleagues profess to be in the dark about what Fetterman is thinking. Though his colleagues are collegial, he frequently sits alone off the Senate floor during votes.

"I really don't have any insight into that," said one Senate Democrat when asked about the party-switch chatter.

There's been speculation within the Senate for months that Fetterman would simply retire rather than mount a difficult reelection campaign in 2028, driven by the widespread view that he doesn't enjoy the job. Fetterman has sidestepped questions about a second term, arguing that it is too early for such questions.

A second Senate Democratic aide added that there was "definitely a concern" about Fetterman but that he still voted "pretty solidly" with Democrats.

"There's a hope that a lot of this is just positioning … and not a real possibility," the aide said. "Hopefully they can find a way to keep him in the fold, but it's not really clear what he actually wants."

A third Senate Democratic aide acknowledged the internal rumors about what he would do while adding that Fetterman and his office are "insular" — making it difficult for anyone outside of his inner circle to know what he's thinking. A fourth added that Senate Democrats weren't taking the speculation that Fetterman could flip "too seriously" for now.

But the aide added that Fetterman could make the caucus' life "harder if he ends up being the 51st vote if the majority is in hand next January."

Republicans, meanwhile, have made it clear that they are trying to recruit Fetterman. McCormick publicly defended him amid the latest round of Democratic backlash, and Majority Leader John Thune told reporters recently that he and other Republican senators have had "conversations" with Fetterman and "would welcome the opportunity" to have him join the GOP.

Only 22% of self-identified Democratic voters in a recent New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena poll have a favorable opinion of Fetterman, compared to 73% of self-identified Republicans.

But it's far from clear that Fetterman could win a GOP primary given that he still votes with Democrats most of the time.

Lamb said Fetterman's inability to prevail in a Democratic primary in 2028 was "as sure a fact as gravity" and added that the senator's path in a GOP primary wouldn't be easy, either.

"I think there are probably people in the state who would run against him if he was in a Republican primary," Lamb said.

Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) said that he takes Fetterman "at his word" that he's a Democrat and said he doubted he'd ever be fully embraced by GOP primary voters. He cited Fetterman's poor ratings from key groups influential on the right, such as the National Rifle Association and National Federation of Independent Business.

"He's a good man. Like I said, he's got courage," he said, before adding, "He's a Democrat and maybe a traditional Democrat, so I don't think that would be something the Republican Party would embrace."

Riley Rogerson contributed to this report.

title: Switzerland publishes a 200-page dossier on Nazi war criminal Mengele nicknamed "Angel of Death"
description: The Swiss federal intelligence service on Thursday published a 200-page dossier on the notorious Nazi war criminal Josef Mengele, the German doctor known as the “Angel of Death” for conducting horrifi...
fullText:
BERLIN (AP) — The Swiss federal intelligence service on Thursday published a 200-page dossier on the notorious Nazi war criminal Josef Mengele, the German doctor known as the "Angel of Death" for conducting horrific medical experiments on prisoners at Auschwitz.

During World War II, Mengele served at the Auschwitz extermination camp in Nazi-occupied Poland, where about 1.1 million people were killed, approximately 1 million of them Jews. He became infamous for carrying out brutal medical experiments on inmates, including children, under the guise of scientific research.

After the war, Mengele obtained a Red Cross travel document under a false identity, allowing him to leave Europe. Like many former Nazi officials, he spent years in hiding in Latin America while being pursued internationally for his crimes. He drowned in 1979 while swimming on the coast of Brazil.

The documents released by Swiss authorities include material provided to police suggesting that Mengele may have returned to Switzerland after initially fleeing Germany, or may have been planning to enter the country under a false name, according to the German news agency dpa.

Historians seeking to establish whether Mengele spent time in Switzerland while being pursued as a war criminal, without Swiss authorities catching him, had long sought access to the files.

Swiss authorities had maintained that the documents should remain sealed until 2071 on security grounds and to protect individuals named in them.

Historian Gérard Wettstein successfully challenged those restrictions before the Federal Administrative Court, leading to the online publication. Some sections have been redacted to protect sources and the personal data of third parties, authorities said.

The dossier was compiled by the police service of the federal prosecutor's office, a predecessor of Switzerland's federal intelligence services, and transferred to the Federal Archives in 2001.

title: Wall Street has thrown in the towel on a quick end to the global oil shock
description: Oil analysts are raising 2027 forecasts as disrupted Middle East shipping, shrinking stockpiles, and inflation risks linger.
fullText:
Wall Street is raising its 2027 oil forecasts with a quick return to normal looking less and less likely.

The longer crude stays elevated, the more pressure builds on consumers, inflation, bonds, and stocks.

Around the time Ben Shelton was polishing off his US Open victory over Carlos Alcaraz in the wee hours of Wednesday morning, the price of oil was making some waves of its own, climbing back above $100 per barrel.

The break into triple digits was weeks in the making. After falling below $80 in early August, oil has been on a mostly uninterrupted climb higher. Any optimism traders have around an Iran-war resolution has fizzled. They're now (re)pricing for a prolonged disruption.

But while $100 is an important psychological milestone, a deeper shift is occurring across Wall Street. There's a growing recognition that the global oil shock may not fade as quickly as investors once hoped.

Perhaps the most drastic reaction to oil's latest spike came from HSBC, which lifted its 2027 Brent forecast by a whopping $20, to $85. The firm's base case is that Strait of Hormuz flows will recover only gradually, continuing the ongoing supply squeeze.

Then there's Goldman Sachs, which raised its 2027 forecast to $80, while also flagging a worst-case scenario of $120 oil where Gulf output remains suppressed.

Not to be outdone, Bank of America said continued Middle East conflict could put oil in a $95-to-$120 range, with $150 a possibility if energy infrastructure is damaged further.

Even if those forecasts remain below oil's current price, Wall Street is now treating triple-digit crude as a realistic outcome rather than a remote risk.

Three forces are combining to sustain the ongoing oil shock. First, the Strait of Hormuz — despite occasional signs of progress — is still operating well below normal capacity.

Second, the oil stockpiles being used to cushion the blow to prices are getting thinner with every delayed shipment.

And finally, while workarounds and new routes have offered relief, they haven't helped enough to avoid a full-blown supply crisis. The old normal is far from being restored, and may never be.

A prolonged stretch of $100-plus crude oil impacts consumers well beyond the gas pump (although that certainly hurts too). It also means higher prices for diesel, jet fuel, and shipping, which can eventually touch nearly everything people spend money on: groceries, deliveries, flights, and utilities, just to name a few.
